subtopic_detail: Persistent watery eye in an infant and the findings that separate it from sight threatening causes
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4 month old girl whose left eye has watered since she was about three weeks old. Her mother says the lashes are stuck together with yellow crust most mornings, but the eye looks clear once she wipes it, and the watering has not changed over the past two months.

The baby feeds well, does not screw the eye up in bright light, and her mother has not seen her rubbing it. The left conjunctiva is white and the cornea is clear and of equal diameter to the right. Red reflexes are present and symmetrical, and gentle pressure over the medial canthus expresses a bead of mucoid material.

data_table.Examination: Increased left tear lake, white conjunctiva, clear cornea, corneal diameters equal, symmetrical red reflexes, mucoid reflux on pressure over the lacrimal sac
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for ophthalmology examination under anaesthesia within one week
options.rationale: Urgent examination under anaesthesia is for suspected infantile glaucoma, which presents with photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding and a corneal diameter larger than the other side, none of which are present here (Source: RCH CPG: The Watering Eye).

options.text: Teach lacrimal sac massage and review at the twelve month check
options.rationale: A white eye with clear cornea, symmetrical red reflexes and mucoid reflux from the sac is uncomplicated congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and around nine in ten resolve spontaneously in the first year, so massage plus lid hygiene and review at twelve months is the plan (Source: RCH CPG: The Watering Eye).

options.text: Prescribe chloramphenicol 0.5 per cent drops six hourly for five days
options.rationale: Topical antibiotic is reserved for a genuinely infected eye with a red conjunctiva and purulent discharge, and crusting alone with a white eye is stagnant tear film rather than conjunctivitis (Source: RCH CPG: The Watering Eye; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Take a conjunctival swab for chlamydia and start oral azithromycin
options.rationale: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis presents at five to fourteen days of life with a red swollen eye and copious discharge, and the near pair distinction from duct obstruction is conjunctival injection and age at onset (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Refer for nasolacrimal duct probing on the next available theatre list
options.rationale: Probing is offered when obstruction persists beyond twelve months or when there is recurrent dacryocystitis, and doing it at four months exposes an infant to anaesthesia for a problem that usually settles itself (Source: RCH CPG: The Watering Eye).

explanation.summary: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction affects up to one in five infants and reflects a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner. The clinical task is not to make that diagnosis but to exclude the two conditions that share the symptom and threaten sight or systemic health: infantile glaucoma and true conjunctivitis. Glaucoma is signalled by photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal haze and an enlarged cornea, and it needs same week ophthalmology assessment. Once those are excluded, massage and observation are enough, with referral reserved for persistence past the first birthday or an episode of dacryocystitis.
key_points: Measure and compare corneal diameters in any infant with a persistently watering eye
Photophobia and blepharospasm push towards glaucoma, not duct obstruction
Mucoid reflux from the lacrimal sac on digital pressure supports duct obstruction
About 90 per cent of duct obstructions resolve without intervention by twelve months
Probing is the intervention after twelve months, not in early infancy
explanation.pearls: An infant corneal diameter above 12 mm, or one more than 0.5 mm larger than the fellow eye, converts a watering eye into a same week ophthalmology referral for suspected infantile glaucoma.

subtopic_detail: Umbilical lesion after cord separation and the features that separate a granuloma from a duct remnant
stem:
You are the doctor in a community child health clinic. A 5 week old boy is brought in because a small lump has appeared where his cord used to be. The cord came away on day 10 and the area has been a little damp on his singlet since.

His mother says there is no smell and the skin around it looks the same colour as the rest of his tummy. He is breastfeeding well and has regained his birth weight. On examination there is a soft pink lesion 4 mm across sitting in the umbilical pit, with no surrounding erythema or induration, and no discharge of urine or faecal material from the site when he cries.

data_table.Examination: Soft pink 4 mm lesion in the umbilical pit with scant serous moisture, periumbilical skin normal in colour and temperature, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Growth: Weight 3.9 kg, back above birth weight since day 12

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply silver nitrate to the lesion weekly until it has flattened
options.rationale: Silver nitrate does shrink the lesion, but it causes chemical burns to the surrounding skin in infants and Australian paediatric practice has moved away from it as first line (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical Granuloma).

options.text: Arrange abdominal ultrasound to look for a persistent urachal remnant
options.rationale: Imaging is driven by discharge of urine or bowel content from the umbilicus, and its absence here makes a patent duct very unlikely (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical Granuloma).

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and gentamicin for two days
options.rationale: Intravenous cover is for omphalitis, whose defining feature is periumbilical erythema, induration or systemic upset, and none of those are present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Apply table salt to the lesion twice daily and review in three days
options.rationale: Topical common salt applied for two to three days is the recommended first line treatment in Australian paediatric practice, is done by the parents at home, and avoids the burn risk of chemical cautery (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical Granuloma).

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for excision of an umbilical remnant
options.rationale: Surgical referral belongs to the bright red firm lesion that persists after salt treatment or discharges enteric or urinary content, which is a vitellointestinal or urachal remnant rather than granulation tissue (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical Granuloma).

explanation.summary: A moist lump appearing in the umbilical pit after cord separation is usually granulation tissue that failed to epithelialise. The two things worth excluding at the bedside cost nothing: periumbilical erythema pointing to omphalitis, and discharge of urine or bowel content pointing to a persistent embryological duct. Australian units now favour topical common salt over silver nitrate because it is as effective, is free, and does not burn the periumbilical skin. Persistence after a course of salt, or a lesion that is deep red and firm rather than soft and pink, is what earns a surgical opinion.
key_points: Ask specifically whether urine or bowel content ever leaks from the umbilicus
Periumbilical erythema or induration converts this into omphalitis needing intravenous antibiotics
Topical salt for two to three days is the Australian first line treatment
Silver nitrate risks chemical burns and is no longer preferred in infants
Refer for surgical review only after failed salt treatment or if a duct remnant is suspected
explanation.pearls: A pinch of table salt held on the lesion for 10 to 30 minutes twice daily for three days flattens most umbilical granulomas, and failure after two such courses is the trigger for surgical referral rather than a repeat course.

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic labial adhesions in a preschool girl and the threshold for treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3 year old girl whose mother noticed while bathing her that the opening between her labia looks sealed over. Her mother is worried it will stop her passing urine.

The girl passes a normal forward stream once or twice every few hours, has never had a urinary tract infection, and has no itch, soreness or bleeding. She is toilet trained by day. On examination the labia minora are joined in the midline by a thin translucent line with a small opening anteriorly, the surrounding skin is normal, and there is no bruising, tear or abnormal pigmentation anywhere on the perineum.

data_table.Examination: Thin translucent midline union of the labia minora with a patent anterior opening, normal perineal skin, no bruising or tears
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure, advise plain water hygiene, and review at her next visit
options.rationale: Adhesions that allow a normal urinary stream and cause no symptoms need no treatment, because they are driven by low oestrogen and separate spontaneously as puberty approaches (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions).

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream to the adhesion nightly for two weeks
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen is reserved for symptomatic adhesions such as urinary obstruction, post void dribbling or recurrent infection, and it commonly causes local irritation and breast budding when used without an indication (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions).

options.text: Separate the adhesion manually in the clinic after topical anaesthetic
options.rationale: Forcible separation is painful, distressing and followed by a high rate of recurrence with denser scar tissue than the original adhesion (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions).

options.text: Refer to the child protection unit for assessment of possible abuse
options.rationale: Labial adhesion is a common finding in this age group and is not in itself a sign of abuse, and referral here is triggered by bruising, tears, disclosure or behavioural change, none of which are present (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for separation under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Surgical separation is the last step for dense adhesions causing urinary retention or recurrent infection that have failed topical oestrogen, not a first move in an asymptomatic child (Source: RCH CPG: Labial Adhesions).

explanation.summary: Labial adhesion is an acquired midline fusion driven by the physiologically low oestrogen state of childhood, and it peaks between one and five years. The decision to treat is symptom driven rather than appearance driven, so the history that matters is the urinary stream, post void dribbling, recurrent infection and local soreness. Most cases separate spontaneously as endogenous oestrogen rises, and parents are much more reassured by being shown the small anterior opening than by a prescription. When treatment is genuinely indicated, topical oestrogen for a short defined course is the first step, with surgical separation kept for failure.
key_points: Confirm a normal urinary stream and absence of post void dribbling before deciding on treatment
Asymptomatic adhesions need reassurance and follow up rather than any active treatment
Topical oestrogen is for obstruction, recurrent infection or persistent soreness
Manual or surgical separation is followed by recurrence with denser scarring
Adhesions alone are not evidence of sexual abuse
explanation.pearls: Adhesions almost always resolve once endogenous oestrogen rises at puberty, so an asymptomatic three year old needs a review appointment rather than oestrogen cream, which itself causes local irritation and breast budding in about one child in five.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear in a toddler with a normal radiograph and normal inflammatory markers
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 20 month old boy who has refused to put his right foot down since yesterday afternoon, when he tripped while running on the grass at his older sister's netball game. His mother says he cried for a minute, then went back to playing, but would not stand up when they got home.

He is afebrile, alert and playing on the trolley. He crawls freely and moves the right hip and knee through full range without complaint, but he cries when the lower shin is squeezed. There is no swelling, warmth or bruising, no joint effusion, and no rash. The radiograph of the tibia and fibula reported by the radiologist shows no fracture.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear on the right, full painless hip and knee range, focal tenderness over the mid to distal tibial shaft, no effusion, warmth or swelling
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); anteroposterior and lateral tibia and fibula radiographs reported as no fracture seen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange hip ultrasound and admit under orthopaedics for joint aspiration
options.rationale: Aspiration follows a septic joint picture of fever, raised inflammatory markers and a hip held still in flexion and external rotation, and full painless hip range with a normal C-reactive protein argues against it (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp).

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and advice to return if still limping in a week
options.rationale: Analgesia alone leaves an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture unprotected, and the child keeps loading a painful limb for the two weeks it takes periosteal reaction to appear (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin after blood cultures are collected
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics treat osteomyelitis, which would show fever, night pain and a raised C-reactive protein rather than an afebrile child with normal markers and a clear mechanism of injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Request urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the right tibia and knee
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging usually needs sedation at this age and adds nothing when the history, focal tibial tenderness and normal markers already define the management (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

options.text: Apply a below knee walking cast and arrange fracture clinic review
options.rationale: An undisplaced spiral tibial fracture in this age group is invisible on the initial film in a large proportion of cases, so a child with a twisting mechanism and focal tibial tenderness is immobilised and reviewed rather than cleared by the radiograph (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler Fracture).

explanation.summary: A toddler who will not weight bear needs the septic joint and osteomyelitis pathway considered first, and here the afebrile state, full painless hip range and normal inflammatory markers close that branch. What remains is an occult undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft, which frequently does not appear on the first radiograph and only becomes visible when periosteal new bone forms at one to two weeks. Treating the clinical picture rather than the film prevents a fortnight of pain and repeated presentations. These fractures are low energy, heal reliably, and do not require operative fixation.
key_points: Normal C-reactive protein with full painless hip movement makes septic arthritis very unlikely
A normal initial radiograph does not exclude an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture
Focal tenderness over the tibial shaft plus a twisting mechanism is enough to treat
Immobilisation with clinic review beats repeat imaging in the first week
Periosteal reaction confirming the fracture appears at about 10 to 14 days
explanation.pearls: Up to half of toddler fractures are radiographically occult on presentation, so a child who localises pain to the tibia after a twisting fall is immobilised on the clinical picture and the confirmatory periosteal reaction is looked for at 10 to 14 days.

subtopic_detail: Scarred preputial ring in a school aged boy versus physiological non retraction
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9 year old boy whose father reports that the end of his penis puffs up like a balloon when he passes urine, and that this has been happening for about six months. Over that time the stream has become thin and sprays sideways, and twice the tip has been sore enough to keep him home from school.

He has never had a urinary tract infection and is otherwise well. On examination the foreskin will not retract at all. The tip is thickened into a firm pale ring that does not stretch when traction is applied, and the visible glans and surrounding skin are not red or inflamed.

data_table.Examination: Non retractile foreskin with a firm pale thickened preputial ring that does not stretch on traction, no erythema of the glans or shaft, no discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes and nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that separation is incomplete and review in twelve months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is right for physiological non retraction, in which the preputial skin is soft and pink and there are no urinary symptoms, and it does not apply once there is scarring with an obstructed stream (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

options.text: Prescribe topical betamethasone twice daily to the tip for six weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid with gentle stretching works well for a soft physiological ring, but a fibrotic pale scar does not soften with steroid and the delay prolongs obstructed voiding (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for circumcision on the elective list
options.rationale: A firm pale scarred preputial ring with ballooning, spraying and recurrent soreness is pathological rather than physiological phimosis, and it is one of the few absolute indications for circumcision in childhood (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care; RACP Circumcision Statement).

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and daily saline soaks
options.rationale: Oral antibiotic treats balanoposthitis, whose near pair feature is a red swollen tender foreskin with purulent discharge rather than a pale avascular fibrotic ring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Teach gentle daily retraction after a warm bath and review in three months
options.rationale: Retraction exercises are appropriate for the soft unscarred foreskin, and forcing a scarred ring risks splitting it and creating further cicatricial scarring (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin Care).

explanation.summary: Most non retractile foreskins in boys are physiological, reflecting incomplete separation of preputial adhesions that completes during the first decade or into adolescence. The distinction that matters is the appearance of the ring: soft, pink and pouting is physiological, while firm, pale and fibrotic is scar. Scarring with obstructed voiding, recurrent soreness or recurrent infection is the pathological form, and it is the setting in which circumcision is genuinely indicated rather than elective. Steroid and stretching should not be used to delay definitive treatment once the ring is fibrotic, because the outcome is repeated splitting and denser scar.
key_points: Physiological non retraction needs no treatment and no examination under anaesthesia
Ballooning alone in a soft unscarred foreskin is not an indication for surgery
A firm pale non stretching ring signals scarring rather than adhesion
Topical corticosteroid is for the soft ring, not the fibrotic one
Scarring with obstructed voiding is an accepted indication for circumcision
explanation.pearls: Topical betamethasone 0.05 per cent twice daily for four to six weeks resolves the majority of soft physiological phimoses, but a pale fibrotic ring predicts steroid failure and should be sent for surgical opinion at the first visit.
